title: Self-help listicle imperative headers
description: This latent fires on short bolded-header imperative bullet points from self-help/advice listicles, especially those recommending well-being techniques like positive self-talk, mindfulness, body language, active listening, and deep breathing. The highest-activating examples are near-formulaic phrasings ('Practice X**: do Y') repeated across many generated lists, typically pairing a bolded category label with a brief instructional clause. Lower-activating cluster members are still advice-list bullet points but drift into more varied, context-specific, or less formulaic content (e.g., relationship-specific tips, negotiation strategies, or narrative asides), lacking the tight, repetitive template structure and canonical wellness vocabulary of the top examples. It is not simply about giving advice in general, nor about the topics themselves (mindfulness, confidence, communication) -- it specifically detects the stereotyped bullet-header format used to enumerate self-improvement tips.

title: Numbered list item markers / balanced-perspective transitions
description: This latent fires on structural tokens that begin enumerated list items (bare numerals like '2.', '3.', '4.') as well as on 'however/that being said/it's also important' style transition sentences that introduce a counterbalancing consideration, typically in advice-giving contexts (e.g., relationship or interpersonal dilemma responses). Included are both the isolated numeral markers that open a new point in a list and the qualifying clauses that pivot from one viewpoint to acknowledge another party's feelings, perspective, or mitigating context. It captures the discourse-structuring function of introducing 'another point' or 'the other side,' not the semantic content of the advice itself. It does NOT include the full substantive content of each list item or argument, nor general list markers unrelated to perspective-balancing (e.g., plain enumerations in factual or technical text without a concessive framing).

title: Assertive 'I'-statement scripts for boundary-setting
description: This latent fires on modeled first-person conversational openers used to express personal needs, discomfort, or boundaries to another person, often in advice-giving contexts that suggest exact phrasing (e.g., 'You could say something like...' followed by an 'I' or 'Can I/we' statement). Included sentences are template utterances beginning with 'I', 'I'd like to', 'Can I', 'Can we', 'Would you mind', etc., that voice feelings ('I feel uncomfortable', 'I'm overwhelmed'), requests to pause/leave/change topic, or gentle assertions of preference, frequently embedded in scripted dialogue suggestions for handling interpersonal friction. It also captures bare sentence fragments ('I', 'Can', 'It was') that are truncated openings of this same script pattern. Excluded are third-person narrations, general advice or analysis about communication strategies that don't themselves model a first-person spoken line (e.g., 'Instead, focus on the specific behavior...'), and unrelated declarative or descriptive statements not framed as something one might say aloud to another person.

title: Moral judgment labeling of interpersonal behavior as harmful
description: This latent fires on evaluative statements that explicitly label someone's behavior, words, or reaction using a negative moral/relational descriptor (e.g., 'unacceptable,' 'hurtful,' 'manipulative,' 'dismissive,' 'abusive,' 'unfair'), typically in a short declarative sentence of the form '[This/His/Her X] was/is [negative adjective(s)].' The highest-activating examples are terse, formulaic condemnations that directly name the wrongdoing without much elaboration or hedging, often stacking two or three negative adjectives together. Lower-activating cluster members still discuss interpersonal conflict and advice-giving contexts but shift toward hedged, explanatory, or interpretive language ('it's possible that,' 'might have,' 'could have led to') or describe situational facts/actions rather than issuing a direct evaluative verdict, so they activate less strongly. The function is specifically the act of pronouncing a clear-cut normative judgment labeling behavior as wrong/harmful, not merely describing conflict or offering neutral advice.

title: Validating the user's actions as reasonable ('You...' affirmations)
description: This latent fires on second-person statements, typically from an advice-giving context (e.g., AITA/relationship advice), that summarize what 'you' did and affirmatively validate it as reasonable, responsible, justified, or praiseworthy. The prototypical pattern is 'You did X, and that's [reasonable/okay/commendable/your right]' or simple declaratives like 'That's a reasonable request' or 'You followed through on your commitment,' functioning to reassure the addressee that their behavior was appropriate and not blameworthy. It includes direct affirmations of rights, boundaries, effort, and responsibility phrased in the second person or as a general validating verdict. It does NOT include sentences that criticize the 'you,' describe a third party's actions or feelings, provide neutral background/factual context without an evaluative validation, or hedge/critique behavior (e.g., 'you didn't respect his boundaries' or descriptions of other people's motivations), which appear only as lower-activating peripheral cluster members rather than the core validating pattern.

title: Empathetic acknowledgment phrase
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic opening phrases where the model explicitly declares empathetic understanding of the user's feelings or situation, typically of the form 'I totally/completely understand [your struggle/frustration/concern/feelings]!'. The top-activating examples are almost all this exact templated exclamation, varying only the intensifier (totally/completely) and the object (your struggle, concern, frustration, dilemma, feelings, or none), usually ending in an exclamation point. The broader cluster includes looser, more elaborated empathetic validation statements ('It's understandable that...', 'That sounds really tough', 'I'm so sorry to hear that...') that serve the same rapport-building function but lack the rigid canned phrasing. It does not include substantive advice, factual claims, or content that merely discusses feelings/situations without the model performing a direct first-person empathy declaration.

title: Empathetic reassurance and self-worth affirmation
description: This latent fires on supportive, second-person closing statements that reassure the reader of their worth, strength, and right to prioritize their own well-being, typically using phrases like 'remember,' 'take care of yourself,' 'you deserve,' and 'you are not alone.' The highest-activating examples are short, formulaic affirmations of self-worth and encouragement (e.g., 'You deserve it,' 'Remember, you are strong and capable') that function as emotional validation or a comforting sign-off, often in advice-giving or supportive contexts like relationship or mental-health advice. Lower-activating cluster members extend this into surrounding advice-giving discourse—situational reasoning, boundary-setting suggestions, or evaluations of who is 'right' in a conflict—that shares the supportive register but is more about analyzing a specific situation than delivering a direct affirmation. Sentences that merely discuss well-being, relationships, or advice-topics without a direct affirming address to 'you' (e.g., neutral situational analysis, third-person descriptions) are not the core pattern, even though they appear in the broader cluster.

title: Rhetorical framing as 'age-old dilemma'
description: This latent fires on stock exclamatory phrases that frame an upcoming topic as a familiar, timeless conflict or quandary, typically of the form 'The age-old debate/dilemma/conundrum of X!' It captures a rhetorical opener used to signal 'this is a well-known type of interpersonal or ethical disagreement' before elaborating on the specifics (e.g., roommate etiquette, sibling rivalry, household chores), and includes near-synonym templates like 'The eternal conundrum...', 'The classic...', and 'The drama of...' used the same way. It does NOT include the substantive discussion or resolution of the dilemma itself, generic transitional or advice sentences (e.g., 'Communication is key'), or unrelated topical content—only the formulaic framing exclamation that introduces the topic as a perennial issue.

title: Benefit-predicting 'this can help' clauses
description: This latent fires on sentences that begin with a demonstrative pronoun (This/This can/This will) followed by a verb like 'help,' 'create,' or 'foster,' predicting a positive relational or emotional outcome (e.g., building trust, diffusing tension, creating rapport, strengthening connections). The highest-activating examples are almost purely the templatic opener itself, often truncated (e.g., 'This can help', 'This can'), showing the latent is most strongly tied to this specific syntactic-semantic frame of forward-looking benefit attribution, typically in advice-giving or relationship-coaching contexts. The broader cluster includes fuller sentences that complete this pattern with concrete benefits (build trust, reduce tension, strengthen bonds, feel supported) and closely related constructions with similar demonstrative-plus-modal-verb structure. It does NOT include sentences that merely discuss relationships or communication without this predictive 'this + modal + positive-outcome' structure, nor does it include sentences expressing uncertainty, describing problems, or giving direct imperative advice without the 'this can/will help' framing.

title: Eliciting the user's input with a follow-up question
description: This latent fires on questions that invite the user to share their own opinion, feelings, or additional details, typically appearing at the end of an assistant response as a prompt for further dialogue. The clearest examples are the exact phrase 'What do you think?' repeated verbatim, but the broader cluster includes varied clarifying or reflective questions such as 'Can you tell me more about...', 'How do you feel about...', and 'What are your goals/priorities/non-negotiables?' that solicit the user's perspective, emotions, or missing context. It is not about the topic of the question (relationships, careers, decisions, etc.) but about the pragmatic function of turning conversational control back to the user by soliciting their input. It excludes purely informational or rhetorical questions that do not seek the user's personal input, as well as declarative statements or advice-giving sentences that don't end in a question inviting response.

title: Enumerated relationship-communication advice
description: This latent fires on list-formatted advice items that recommend communication strategies for resolving interpersonal conflicts (e.g., 'have an open and honest conversation', 'set boundaries', 'use "I" statements', 'express your feelings'). The top-activating examples are the bare numeral/period tokens ("2.", "3.", "4.") that mark the start of such enumerated advice lists, showing the latent tracks the structural position of list items in advice-giving responses. The broader cluster confirms this: nearly all sentences are discrete numbered or bulleted recommendations, often with a bolded lead phrase followed by a colon, advising the reader to talk to, listen to, empathize with, or set limits with a partner, family member, friend, or colleague. It does not include general narrative description, emotional venting, or advice that isn't packaged as a discrete list step -- the defining feature is the list-item/enumeration format applied to relational communication guidance, not merely the topic of relationships.

title: Recommending deferential compliance
description: This latent fires on sentences that advise accepting an authority's or another party's request while also respecting an established boundary or rule set by a third party. It captures a specific advisory pattern combining two elements: compliance with one party's wishes and deference to another's limits or norms, typically phrased as a directive or recommendation. It is not simply about agreement or politeness in general, nor about refusing requests or resolving conflicts between competing demands through negotiation. What distinguishes it from generic advice-giving is the dual structure of 'accept X's request AND respect Y's boundary,' rather than a single unqualified recommendation.

title: Colon-plus-numbered-list preamble
description: This latent fires on the transitional phrase that introduces an upcoming enumerated list, typically ending in a colon followed by the start of a numbered (or occasionally bulleted) list item such as '1.' or '1. **'. Included sentences are short lead-in fragments like 'Here are some suggestions:', 'Here's why:', 'Here are some points to consider:', or 'Let's break it down:' immediately followed by the first list marker, regardless of the specific topic being introduced. It activates most strongly on the barest, most templated versions of this construction (just the lead-in phrase plus '1.'), and less strongly when the lead-in is more elaborated or followed by actual list content. It does NOT fire on the substantive content of the list items themselves, on advice-giving sentences that lack this colon-plus-list-marker structure (e.g. 'However, it's essential to take a step back...'), or on general discourse markers that don't precede an enumerated list.

title: Listing concrete resource options (services/platforms/programs)
description: This latent fires on list items or clauses that enumerate specific, named or generically-typed resources, services, platforms, or venues a person could use to address a need—e.g., 'online forums,' 'VolunteerMatch,' 'Uber Eats,' 'community centers,' 'BetterHelp,' 'food banks.' The pattern is a suggestion-giving format, typically bulleted or in a short declarative sentence, that names concrete options (often 2-3 alternatives joined by 'or') such as gig-economy apps, tutoring services, charities, online course platforms, or crisis hotlines, functioning as an actionable resource directory within advice-giving text. It is NOT simply any advice or suggestion sentence in general (e.g., abstract recommendations like 'seek professional help,' 'communicate with your partner,' or 'find alternative solutions' without naming concrete services/platforms) and NOT sentences focused on interpersonal negotiation, compromise, or relational strategy even if phrased as suggestions—those score low unless they include a named resource/platform/service list.

title: Reassuring normalization / universal validation statements
description: This latent fires on short, affirming reassurance statements that normalize a person's trait, feeling, mistake, or experience by framing it as universally human, common, or valuable ('Everyone is unique and special', 'That's a common human experience', 'We all make mistakes', 'Nobody is perfect'). The included sentences are typically brief, emotionally supportive assertions delivered directly to or about a listener, emphasizing shared humanity, individuality, or inherent worth, often as a therapeutic or comforting rhetorical move (e.g., in advice-giving contexts) rather than as substantive argument or explanation. It is distinguished from merely topically similar advice-column sentences that give specific situational reasoning, hedges, or caveats about a particular scenario (e.g., 'It's possible he's not emotionally invested' or 'This could be due to a variety of reasons') -- those explain or speculate about a specific case, whereas this cluster asserts general, universalizing reassurance detached from case-specific reasoning. Sentences that merely describe benefits or list considerations without the 'you/we are all normal and valuable' validating framing are excluded, even if they share warm or supportive tone.

title: AITA-style moral verdict framing
description: This latent fires on the characteristic rhetorical markers of Reddit 'Am I the Asshole' (AITA/WIBTA) style moral judgments: the literal question tag itself ('AITA?', 'So, AITA?', 'WIBTA?'), hedged partial-agreement phrases like 'Not entirely' that soften a verdict, and surrounding sentences that render a nuanced not-quite-yes-or-no judgment about whether someone is at fault (e.g., 'you're not entirely in the wrong', 'NTA', 'I don't think you're the asshole but...'). The top-activating examples are almost purely the bare interrogative/hedge tokens themselves, while the broader cluster includes fuller verdict sentences that qualify blame, offer caveats ('That being said...', 'However...'), or explicitly weigh both sides before delivering a moral ruling. It does not include general advice-giving, factual explanations, or moral reasoning outside this specific hedged-verdict/question format -- e.g., sentences that just state opinions or give instructions without invoking the asshole/blame framing or a partial-agreement hedge are excluded.
